response.text:
Tom’s early life.

Let us skip a number of years.

London was fifteen hundred years old, and a great town—for that day—some said it held a hundred thousand souls. The streets were very narrow, crooked, and dirty, most of all near London Bridge, where Tom Canty lived. The houses were of wood, shouldering outward as they climbed; skeletons of strong criss-cross beams, with the spaces filled and plastered; the beams painted red or blue or black, to the owner’s taste. Small diamond-paned windows opened outward, on hinges, like doors.

Tom’s father dwelt up a foul little pocket out of Pudding Lane, called Offal Court. The house was small, decayed, and rickety, and packed with wretchedly poor families. Canty’s tribe had a room on the third floor. The mother and father owned a sort of bedstead in the corner; but Tom, his grandmother, and his twin sisters, Bet and Nan, had all the floor, and might sleep where they chose. There were the remnants of a blanket or two, and bundles of ancient and dirty straw—no true beds, for they were not organised; mornings the stuff was kicked into a heap, and at night each made his selection for service.

Bet and Nan were fifteen—good-hearted girls, unclean, ragged, and profoundly ignorant; their mother was like them. But the father and the grandmother were a couple of fiends. They got drunk when they could; then they fought—each other or any that came in the way; they cursed and swore always, drunk or sober. John Canty was a thief, and his mother a beggar. They made beggars of the children, but failed to make thieves of them. Among, but not of, that dreadful rabble, was a good old priest whom the King had turned out of house and home with a pension of a few farthings; he would get the children aside and teach them right ways secretly. Father Andrew taught Tom a little Latin, and how to read and write; he would have done the same for the girls, but they were afraid of the jeers of their friends, who could not have endured so queer an accomplishment.

All Offal Court was such another hive: drunkenness, riot, and brawling the order there every night and nearly all night long; broken heads were as common as hunger. Yet little Tom was not unhappy. He had a hard time of it, but did not know it; it was the sort of time all the Offal Court boys had, therefore he supposed it the correct and comfortable thing. When he came home empty-handed, his father would curse him and thrash him; when he was done, the awful grandmother would do it again and improve on it; and away in the night his starving mother would steal to him with any miserable scrap or crust she had saved by going hungry herself—often caught in that treason, and soundly beaten for it.

Tom begged only so much as might save him, for the laws against mendicancy were stringent, and penalties heavy; and he put in much time listening to good Father Andrew’s charming old tales and legends of giants and fairies, dwarfs and genii, enchanted castles, and gorgeous kings and princes. His head grew full of these wonders; and many a night, as he lay in the dark on his scant and offensive straw, tired, hungry, and smarting from a thrashing, he unleashed his imagination and forgot his aches in delicious picturings of the charmed life of a petted prince in a regal palace. One desire came in time to haunt him day and night: it was to see a real prince, with his own eyes. He spoke of it once to comrades; they jeered and scoffed so unmercifully that he kept his dream thereafter to himself.

He often read the priest’s old books and had him explain and enlarge upon them; by-and-by his dreamings and readings wrought changes in him. His dream-people were so fine that he began to lament his dirt and rags, and to wish to be clean and better clad. He played in the mud as before, enjoying it too; but, instead of splashing in the Thames solely for the sport, he found an added value in the washings and cleansings it afforded.

Tom could always find something going on about the Maypole in Cheapside, and at the fairs; now and then London had a military parade when some famous unfortunate was carried prisoner to the Tower, by land or boat. One summer’s day he saw poor Anne Askew and three men burned at the stake in Smithfield, and heard an ex-Bishop preach a sermon to them which did not interest him. Yes, Tom’s life was varied and pleasant enough, on the whole.

By-and-by his reading and dreaming about princely life so wrought upon him that he began to _act_ the prince unconsciously. His speech and manners grew curiously ceremonious and courtly, to the vast admiration and amusement of his intimates. His influence among the young people increased day by day; in time they looked up to him with a wondering awe as a superior being. He seemed to know so much; he could do and say such marvellous things; and withal he was so deep and wise. The boys reported Tom’s sayings and doings to their elders; presently these discussed Tom Canty too, and regarded him as most gifted and extraordinary. Full-grown folk brought their perplexities for solution, and were often astonished at the wit and wisdom of his decisions. In fact, he was become a hero to all who knew him—except his own family; these only saw nothing in him.

Privately Tom organised a royal court. He was the prince; his special comrades were guards, chamberlains, equerries, lords and ladies in waiting, and the royal family. Daily the mock prince was received with ceremonials borrowed from his romantic readings; daily the affairs of the mimic kingdom were debated in council; daily his mimic highness issued decrees to his imaginary armies, navies, and viceroyalties. After which he went forth in his rags to beg a few farthings, ate his poor crust, took his customary cuffs and abuse, and then stretched himself upon his handful of foul straw and resumed his empty grandeurs in his dreams.

And still his desire to look but once upon a real prince, in the flesh, grew, day by day and week by week, till at last it absorbed all other desires and became the one passion of his life.

One January day, on his usual begging tour, he tramped despondently about Mincing Lane and Little East Cheap, hour after hour, barefooted and cold, looking in at cook-shop windows and longing for the dreadful pork-pies and other deadly inventions displayed there—for to him these were dainties fit for the angels; that is, judging by the smell they were, for it had never been his good luck to own and eat one. There was a cold drizzle; the atmosphere murky; it was a melancholy day. At night Tom reached home so wet and tired and hungry that it was not possible for his father and grandmother to observe his forlorn condition and not be moved—after their fashion; wherefore they gave him a brisk cuffing at once and sent him to bed. Long his pain and hunger, and the swearing and fighting in the building, kept him awake; at last his thoughts drifted to far romantic lands, and he fell asleep among jewelled and gilded princelings who lived in vast palaces and had servants salaaming before them or flying to execute their orders. And then, as usual, he dreamed that _he_ was a princeling himself.

All night long the glories of his royal estate shone upon him; he moved among great lords and ladies, in a blaze of light, breathing perfumes, drinking in delicious music, answering the reverent obeisances of the glittering throng with here a smile and there a nod of his princely head.

And when he awoke in the morning and looked upon the wretchedness about him, his dream had had its usual effect—it had intensified the sordidness of his surroundings a thousandfold. Then came bitterness, and heart-break, and tears.
